History: Unified under the pharaohs around 3100 BC, Egypt endured through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms, building an empire that stretched into Canaan and Nubia. It later fell to Assyria, Persia, Greece, and Rome, but its monuments and records outlasted every conqueror.
Culture: Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs, built pyramids and temples on a monumental scale, and advanced medicine, astronomy, and administration. The annual Nile flood made farming predictable and supported one of the ancient world's most stable states.
Religion: Egypt worshipped many gods, chief among them Ra, Osiris, Isis, and Horus, and treated the pharaoh as a divine king. Belief in judgment after death shaped its tombs, mummification, and funerary texts.
BibleConnection: Abraham visited Egypt in famine; Joseph rose to vizier there; Israel spent centuries in Egypt before the Exodus, the defining deliverance of the Old Testament. Later kings allied with Egypt, refugees fled there after Jerusalem's fall, and Joseph and Mary took the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Zipporah; Mizraim
RelatedEvents: Abram in Egypt; Joseph and His Brothers; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Region: Eastern Mediterranean coast and hill country, between Egypt and Mesopotamia
History: Canaan was a land of independent city-states rather than one empire, fought over by Egypt and Mesopotamia. God promised it to Abraham's descendants, and under Joshua Israel conquered and settled it, then struggled for generations to hold it against its peoples.
Culture: Canaanites farmed, traded, and built walled cities, and wrote in an early alphabet that influenced later scripts. Their pottery, idols, and fortifications appear throughout the archaeology of Israel.
Religion: Canaanite religion centered on El and Baal, with Asherah and ritual practices Scripture repeatedly condemns, including child sacrifice. Israel's recurring turn to Baal worship is one of the Old Testament's persistent warnings.
BibleConnection: Canaan is the Promised Land of the patriarchs, the land of the conquest under Joshua, and the setting of Judges. Its peoples and gods are the constant test of Israel's faithfulness to the covenant.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Jacob; Joshua; Rahab; Caleb; Melchizedek
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Walls of Jericho; Crossing the Jordan

Region: Southern coastal plain of Canaan: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath
History: The Philistines were part of the Sea Peoples who settled the coast around 1200 BC, organized in a league of five cities. They fought Israel from the days of the judges through David, captured the ark briefly, and were eventually absorbed by the empires that followed.
Culture: Philistine pottery, iron-working, and Aegean roots set them apart from their Canaanite neighbors. Their cities were wealthy trading ports ruled by lords called serens.
Religion: The Philistines worshipped Dagon, Ashtoreth, and Baal-zebub. The ark's capture and Dagon's fall before it (1 Samuel 5) became a vivid sign of God's supremacy over their gods.
BibleConnection: Philistia is the great rival of Israel's early history: Samson's enemy, the home of Goliath, and the power David fought before and after becoming king. The word Palestine derives from Philistia.
RelatedEvents: Samson and Delilah; David and Goliath

Region: Northern Levantine coast: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos
History: Phoenician city-states dominated Mediterranean trade, founding colonies as far as Carthage. They were never a single empire, but their ships, timber, and purple dye made them indispensable partners of Israel's kings.
Culture: Phoenicians are credited with spreading the alphabet that became the ancestor of Greek and Latin scripts. Their cedar timber built temples and palaces across the region.
Religion: Phoenician religion honored Baal, Astarte, and Eshmun, with rites Scripture condemns. Jezebel, daughter of Sidon's king, brought Baal worship to Israel's court with devastating effect.
BibleConnection: Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple; Jezebel's marriage to Ahab imported Baal worship; Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Syrophoenician woman's faith drew his praise.

History: Aramean kingdoms, chiefly Damascus, rose after the Bronze Age collapse and contested the land east and north of Israel. Aram fought Israel under Ben-Hadad and Hazael, allied with it at times, and finally fell to Assyria in 732 BC.
Culture: Aramaic, the language of the Arameans, became the lingua franca of the Near East and the everyday language of Jesus' world. Aramean trade and diplomacy connected Mesopotamia with the Levant.
Religion: Arameans worshipped Hadad (Rimmon), the storm god, among others. Naaman, commander of Aram's army, was healed of leprosy after washing in the Jordan at Elisha's word.
BibleConnection: Aram is both enemy and neighbor in Kings: wars with Ahab and Jehoram, the siege of Samaria, and Naaman's healing, which showed God's mercy reaching beyond Israel.

Region: Highlands east of the Dead Sea
History: Moab, descended from Lot according to Genesis, was a small kingdom east of the Dead Sea that alternated between war and uneasy peace with Israel. King Mesha's revolt against Israel is recorded both in 2 Kings 3 and on his own victory stele.
Culture: Moabites farmed the highlands and controlled the King's Highway trade route. Their language was closely related to Hebrew, and their royal inscriptions are among the closest parallels to biblical Hebrew.
Religion: Moab worshipped Chemosh, to whom kings offered sacrifices, including, at least once, a king's own son in wartime desperation. Ruth the Moabitess, who left Moab to follow Naomi's God, became an ancestor of David.
BibleConnection: Balak of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel; Ruth came from Moab; and the plains of Moab are where Moses died within sight of the Promised Land.
RelatedPeople: Ruth; Naomi; Boaz; Lot; Balaam; Balak
RelatedFinds: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone); Balaam Inscription (Deir Alla Inscription)

Region: East of the Jordan, around modern Amman
History: The Ammonites, descended from Lot's son Ben-Ammi, held the land east of the Jordan around their capital Rabbah. They clashed with Israel from the judges through David, who captured Rabbah, and survived as a small state into the Persian period.
Culture: Ammon shared the language and material culture of its neighbors Moab and Israel, and its capital Rabbah was a fortified trade center on the King's Highway.
Religion: Ammon worshipped Molech (Milcom), whose rites included child sacrifice, which the Law of Moses strictly forbade. Solomon's Ammonite wives brought Molech's worship into Jerusalem itself.
BibleConnection: Jephthah defeated Ammon; Saul's first victory as king was against Ammon's siege of Jabesh-gilead; David's war with Ammon frames the Bathsheba story.

Region: South of the Dead Sea, from the Arabah to the Red Sea
History: Edom, descended from Esau, occupied the rugged land south of the Dead Sea and controlled the copper mines of the Arabah and the Red Sea port of Ezion-geber. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness, warred with Judah's kings, and was later displaced by the Nabataeans; its people, the Idumeans, included Herod the Great's family.
Culture: Edomites built their capital at Bozrah and the mountain stronghold of Petra's region, living by mining, herding, and tolls on the trade routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean.
Religion: Edom worshipped Qos as its chief god. The prophet Obadiah pronounced judgment on Edom for standing by, and even joining in, when Jerusalem fell.
BibleConnection: Edom is Esau's land, the brother-nation that became Israel's rival: the birthright story, the refused passage, and Obadiah's oracle all turn on that brotherhood.

Region: Anatolia (modern Turkey), with influence into Syria and Canaan
History: The Hittites built one of the Bronze Age's great empires from their capital Hattusa, fighting Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and concluding the earliest surviving peace treaty. After the empire's fall around 1200 BC, smaller Neo-Hittite states survived in Syria for centuries.
Culture: Hittites pioneered iron-working, codified laws, and drew up detailed treaties and covenants. Their treaty forms — preamble, history, stipulations, blessings and curses — closely parallel the structure of the biblical covenants.
Religion: Hittite religion embraced a thousand gods, led by the storm god Tarhunt and the sun goddess Arinna. Their rituals and legal texts show a world of oaths, purity rules, and treaty obligations.
BibleConnection: Hittites appear in the patriarchal stories: Ephron the Hittite sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah, and Uriah the Hittite was the husband of Bathsheba. Hittite treaty patterns help explain the shape of God's covenants with Israel.

History: Assyria rose from a city-state on the Tigris to the Near East's first true empire, conquering the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and deporting its people. Its siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC failed, and Nineveh itself fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC.
Culture: Assyrians built vast palaces and libraries — Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh — and administered their empire with roads, officials, and mass deportations.
Religion: Assyria's chief god was Assur, with Ishtar of Nineveh and other gods of war and fertility. Its kings presented conquest as divine mandate, and their annals record cruelty as policy.
BibleConnection: Assyria is the rod of God's judgment in Isaiah and the repentant city of Jonah's preaching. Its fall, celebrated by Nahum, showed that even the mightiest empire answers to God.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Fall of Samaria
RelatedFinds: Sennacherib Prism (Taylor Prism); Lachish Reliefs; Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III; Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III

History: Babylon, heir of Sumer and Akkad, reached its height under Hammurabi and again under Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BC without a battle.
Culture: Babylon gave the world Hammurabi's law code, advanced astronomy and mathematics, the Hanging Gardens tradition, and the ziggurat — the stepped temple tower behind the Babel story.
Religion: Babylon worshipped Marduk above a large pantheon, with Ishtar, Shamash, and Nabu among the chief gods. Its priests read omens in the stars and livers, a practice Daniel's God repeatedly overruled.
BibleConnection: Babylon is both a place and a symbol in Scripture: the tower of Babel, the exile that reshaped Israel's faith, Daniel's court, and the 'Babylon' of Revelation standing for every proud power opposed to God.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Daniel in the Lions' Den
RelatedFinds: Babylonian Chronicle (Nebuchadnezzar's Chronicle); Code of Hammurabi; Nabonidus Cylinder; Jehoiachin's Rations Tablets; Al-Yahudu Tablets

Region: Iran plateau to the Mediterranean, capital Susa and Persepolis
History: Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, the largest the ancient world had yet seen, stretching from India to Greece. His edict let the Jewish exiles return and rebuild the temple; later kings Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes framed the world of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.
Culture: Persia administered its empire through satrapies, royal roads, and a policy of tolerance toward local customs and gods. Its postal system and coinage knit together peoples from three continents.
Religion: Persian kings promoted Ahura Mazda, the wise lord of Zoroastrian teaching, while tolerating the religions of their subjects. The empire's tolerance is what made the return from exile possible.
BibleConnection: Persia is the setting of the return: Cyrus's decree, the temple's rebuilding, Esther in Susa, and Nehemiah's wall. Isaiah calls Cyrus God's anointed, the pagan king who serves God's purpose.
RelatedPeople: Cyrus the Great; Mordecai; Nehemiah; Ezra; Elam
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Esther Saves Her People; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple; Ezra Reads the Law

Region: Greek mainland, Aegean islands, and Alexander's eastern empire
History: Greek city-states gave the West philosophy, drama, and democracy, and Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture across the East. After Alexander, his successors ruled the world of the Maccabees, and Greek became the language in which the New Testament was written.
Culture: Greece prized reason, rhetoric, athletics, and art, and its language became the common tongue of the eastern Mediterranean. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, carried Scripture to the wider world.
Religion: Greeks worshipped Zeus, Athena, Apollo, and a host of gods on Olympus and in every city. Paul found Athens full of idols and an altar 'to an unknown god,' which became his opening to preach Christ.
BibleConnection: Daniel foresaw Greece as the goat that shatters Persia's ram; the New Testament was written in Greek; and Paul's missionary journeys carried the gospel through the Greek cities of Corinth, Athens, Philippi, and Ephesus.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Conversion of Paul
RelatedFinds: Gallio Inscription; Corinth Bema (Judgment Seat); Politarch Inscription; Erastus Inscription

Region: Italian peninsula to an empire around the Mediterranean
History: Rome grew from a city-state to a republic and then an empire that ruled the whole Mediterranean world, including Judea from 63 BC. Its roads, laws, and peace — the Pax Romana — form the backdrop of the entire New Testament.
Culture: Rome built roads, aqueducts, and cities on a scale never seen before, spread Latin law and citizenship, and absorbed Greek art and learning. Its engineering and administration held a vast empire together for centuries.
Religion: Romans worshipped Jupiter, Mars, and the emperor himself, whose cult demanded loyalty from every subject. Christians' refusal to call Caesar lord was one reason for their persecution.
BibleConnection: Jesus was born under Caesar Augustus's census, crucified under Pontius Pilate, and Paul appealed to Caesar and was imprisoned in Rome itself. The empire that killed the apostles also carried their message to the ends of the earth.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; Paul in Rome
RelatedFinds: Pilate Stone; Herodium (Herod's Tomb); Ephesus Theater; Sergius Paulus Inscription
